power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Psychotherapy generally begins with a person who has a problem and needs help resolving it.
Deconstructive Inquiry (DI) examines how the struggle to resolve a difficulty can form the apparent self who must overcome it.
This conceptual paper draws on a relational ontology, which understands things as organized patterns of relations.
The self who must overcome fear, for example, takes shape through judging, resisting, and trying to escape fear.
This activity is experienced as someone separate from the feeling and responsible for ending it.
I call this formation centering.
Comparison with a remembered past or imagined future can sustain the struggle by making present life unacceptable until the person changes.
DI proposes that the effort and its apparent controller can become recognizable as the same activity.
The division need not continue, even while fear remains and the person responds to what needs attention.
A composite clinical vignette illustrates this possibility and shows how the therapist's need to prove helpful can reinforce the client's struggle.
I also propose that insight changes the knowledge shaping later encounters, allowing change to persist without requiring the person to recall or repeat the insight.
Comparisons with other therapies examine whether a separate observing self remains when therapy succeeds.
The paper considers how cultural expectations shape these struggles and how therapists and supervisors can participate in sustaining or questioning them.
Maya was a 27-year-old graduate student who came to therapy because she felt "stuck in every part of life."
She struggled to complete assignments, was unsure about a relationship, and resented her parents.
She compared herself constantly with peers who seemed to be finishing degrees, marrying, and starting careers.
"I know what I need to do," she said in the first session.
"I just don't do it."
Maya is a composite drawn from situations that recur in my practice.
Details have been altered and combined so that the account describes no identifiable client.
Maya understood a great deal about herself.
She could explain how her parents' expectations fed her perfectionism and how fear of failure led to procrastination.
However, knowing why she struggled could become another reason to judge herself.
If she understood this much, why was she still like this?
A plan might help her complete an assignment, but following it could also become a test of whether she was capable of changing.
Each unfinished assignment then seemed to confirm that something was wrong with her.
Maya needed help writing the paper, yet our work kept returning to what her difficulty writing it seemed to say about her.
As we returned to this impasse, I began to feel ineffective and a little irritated.
I prepared more structured interventions, hoping to help Maya find a way forward.
That was a reasonable response to her difficulty, but I was also measuring my competence by whether she improved.
Her lack of progress made her seem like a resistant client and me a therapist who had not found the right intervention.
We both needed something from her improvement.
She needed evidence that she could change, and I needed evidence that I could help her change.
Counseling generally begins with a person who has a problem.
The counselor's task is to help the person resolve it.
Maya's difficulty suggested a further question.
Finishing an assignment had become a way to prove that she was capable, while failing to finish it confirmed that she needed fixing.
Each new strategy gave her another opportunity to succeed or fail at changing herself.
The question is whether helping Maya finish her assignments was also reinforcing the idea that she needed to fix herself.
I created Deconstructive Inquiry (DI) to examine how a self and its problem form together.
I first presented the framework in the consciousness literature (Greenleaf, 2025).
text.formatted: I first presented the framework in the consciousness literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Greenleaf, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Thought divides experience into fear and a self who appears to stand apart from it.
When thought judges fear as weakness and demands strength, this self seems to exist already, as someone weak who has fear to overcome.
But the judgment and the demand are what form this self: they make fear the weakness to correct and the self the weak one who must correct it.
Thought invents the self.
I call this the self-problem relation.
The self described here is the one who must overcome fear, defend a belief, or bring uncertainty under control, not the whole person.
The person's bodily life, memory, relationships, responsibilities, and ability to act extend beyond this struggle and can continue when the self no longer forms.
The same pattern formed when Maya compared her life with the life she believed she should already have.
The comparison made her present life a problem to correct and formed the self who was behind and had to catch up.
I call this claiming of experience centering.
A feeling, belief, or situation is experienced as something a self has and must change or protect.
The claiming forms the claimer.
For Maya, that self took shape through measuring her life against an expectation and trying to catch up.
The life she believed she should have was already shaping how she understood her life now and what she felt she had to do.
The question for counseling is whether this division can end while the client continues to feel and respond to what is happening.
Maya might still feel afraid and work on the assignment without treating her fear as proof that she needs fixing.
I also examine how the therapist's responses and the client's social circumstances shape this division.
Through this division, the person may feel that life cannot go on until the problem is solved.
I use suffering to name the struggle between life as it is and life as the person believes it should or must be.
Someone may believe they should already be happier or further along, or that they must recover the happiness they once had.
They may also believe they can be happy only when a present difficulty ends.
Their life now is judged against a remembered past or imagined future.
Trying to hold on to present pleasure can create the same struggle, as the person fears losing it.
Fear and grief can already be intense and require care.
Someone hurt by rejection may also believe they cannot go on with life until the hurt is gone.
The hurt then becomes the obstacle to living, and the self becomes the one who must overcome it.
The effort to escape the hurt keeps forming the self whose life must wait for the hurt to end.
The same division can form around a belief.
A conclusion such as "I am intelligent" may become a position the person must maintain or defend.
The believing forms the believer: the self whose position must be protected.
A challenge to the belief then feels like a challenge to that self.
The self seems to have existed before the struggle, but it takes shape through the effort to defend the belief.
This is the owner-owned division: the apparent separation between the self and the belief it must defend.
Centering can also take the form of a demand for certainty.
Someone insists, "I need to know that nothing will go wrong before I can relax."
They feel uncertain now and believe they can be at ease only in a future where everything is secure.
This demand forms the uncertain self, the one who must bring uncertainty under control.
That self seems to stand apart from the search, but it takes shape through the search itself.
The effort to become certain is uncertainty continuing in this form.
We use "I" and "my" for ordinary purposes.
"My keys" identifies which keys belong to someone.
"My anxiety" may simply tell the therapist how the client feels.
Using "my" for both does not mean feelings are owned like keys.
To tell whether centering is occurring, the therapist looks at what happens as the client tries to change the feeling.
A client wants relief because anxiety keeps them awake and they need sleep.
They do not believe that ending the anxiety would prove their competence or let their life begin.
Even so, as they try to end it, they may experience themselves as someone who stands apart from the anxiety and must control it.
That is centering.
The separate self is the anxious effort itself, not someone behind it.
Therapist and client can examine how that self forms while also working on sleep.
The inquiry itself should not become another demand: "Now I must stop struggling."
Maya's life extends beyond the struggle to put herself right.
Her bodily activity, memory, and relationships support her abilities and responsibilities.
These remain whether or not an unfinished paper becomes proof that she is a failure.
A person can still act when a self-problem no longer forms.
If they recognize danger, they can leave.
If a condition needs treatment, they can seek care.
Life continues without the conflict thought creates between what is and what it demands should be. Gallagher (2000) uses agency to name the sense that one is causing an action.
text.formatted: Life continues without the conflict thought creates between what is and what it demands should be. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Gallagher (2000)</ref> uses agency to name the sense that one is causing an action.

text.text: He uses ownership to name the sense that one is undergoing an experience.
Neither sense, by itself, establishes a separate self who stands apart from the activity and directs it.
In DI, ownership names the apparent separation between an experience and the self who takes shape through the effort to change or protect it.
Table 1 defines the terms used in what follows.
Note.
Each term is developed in the section where it first becomes important.
Ontology is an account of what reality consists of.
A substance-based account begins with separate things and explains how they interact.
A relational ontology understands the things themselves as organized patterns of relations.
A whirlpool makes this easier to picture.
It is water moving in a particular pattern.
Different water passes through, but the whirlpool continues while that pattern holds together.
The whirlpool is real as the organized movement of the water.
The water itself is an organization of interacting molecules.
Each water molecule is a pattern of relations among two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
The atoms, in turn, are organized patterns involving nuclei and electrons.
Relational ontology extends this account to those constituents as well: at each level, things are understood through the relations that constitute them.
DI applies this account to the self who must solve a problem.
When thought judges fear as weakness and demands strength, it forms the self who must overcome fear.
This self is the pattern of judging fear and demanding its end.
It continues as long as that pattern continues.
Fear can remain when the self who must overcome it no longer forms.
DI uses grains to examine this change.
A grain specifies which relations a description preserves and which details it leaves aside.
We can describe the circulation of a whirlpool or examine the movements of the water that sustain it.
Each description must track the actual organization of the moving water.
Mereology is the study of parts and wholes.
This use of grain draws on refinement mereology.
A finer pattern refines a coarser one when the coarser organization can be recovered by leaving aside some of the finer detail.
The relations that define that organization must be preserved.
An account of individual water movements, for example, must still account for the circulation identified as the whirlpool.
DI draws on this approach to examine which relations The recognitional-categorical grain describes what the employee experiences.
It is recognitional because their knowledge is operating as the experience.
It is categorical because the experience is of a particular kind: the employee hears criticism and feels fear.
They can feel afraid without naming the feeling or being able to explain why.
Within DI, consciousness is this experience as it occurs, including the words, their meaning, and the fear.
Thought can also divide this experience into fear and a self who appears to stand apart from it.
Fear becomes "mine to control."
The employee may feel that life cannot begin until fear ends, or that they must keep fear away to remain acceptable.
This demand makes fear the problem to overcome and forms the self who must overcome it.
DI calls this claiming of experience the centering grain.
The claiming forms the claimer.
The self seems to direct the effort to end fear, but it is that effort experienced as someone separate from the feeling.
The centering grain describes this formation of an apparent owner and the feeling it must control.
These grains describe the same encounter.
They are not steps that must happen one after
DI proposes that consciousness is its content (Greenleaf, 2025).
text.formatted: DI proposes that consciousness is its content <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Greenleaf, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Seeing a color, hearing a voice, remembering an event, and feeling afraid are consciousness occurring.
The content includes how each experience feels.
Consciousness is not something separate that contains these experiences.
DI explains them as recognition: knowledge operating as what is seen, heard, remembered, or felt.
As U. G. Krishnamurti (1988) put it, "Without knowledge no experience of any kind is possible" (p. 51).
text.formatted: As U. G. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Krishnamurti (1988)</ref> put it, "Without knowledge no experience of any kind is possible" (p. 51).

text.text: Much of this knowledge is learned, and it can change.
If the employee described earlier finds that the supervisor now listens and offers help, a later question may feel less threatening.
The supportive encounter can change the knowledge through which later questions are understood and felt.
Knowledge, in this account, can also be inherited. Fendt (2006) found that rats with no prior exposure to predator odors responded defensively to predator urine but not to herbivore urine.
text.formatted: Knowledge, in this account, can also be inherited. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Fendt (2006)</ref> found that rats with no prior exposure to predator odors responded defensively to predator urine but not to herbivore urine.

text.text: This finding documents an unlearned defensive response.
DI proposes that inherited knowledge can also operate as the experience of danger.
Experience therefore need not depend on prior learning or language.
I use thought in this broad sense of knowledge operating, whether inherited or learned and whether or not words are involved.
Language is one form of learned knowledge, and it can affect what people notice and distinguish (Lupyan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Language is one form of learned knowledge, and it can affect what people notice and distinguish <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Lupyan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Russian speakers, for example, distinguished certain shades of blue more quickly when the shades fell into different categories in their language (Winawer et al., 2007), although later findings show limits to this effect (Martinovic et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Russian speakers, for example, distinguished certain shades of blue more quickly when the shades fell into different categories in their language <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Winawer et al., 2007)</ref>, although later findings show limits to this effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Martinovic et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These findings support a role for language in perception.
DI goes further: the knowledge operating in recognition is the experience itself.
As Maya pictured her classmates completing their work, her body tensed.

What she had learned about achievement and falling behind was operating as her fear. Barrett's (2017) theory of constructed emotion offers a related account: categorizing bodily sensations through past experience is part of how an emotion forms.
text.formatted: What she had learned about achievement and falling behind was operating as her fear. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Barrett's (2017)</ref> theory of constructed emotion offers a related account: categorizing bodily sensations through past experience is part of how an emotion forms.

text.text: DI also examines how an apparent owner forms within this experience.
When Maya treats fear as proof that she cannot manage her life, fear becomes a defect to correct, and the self becomes the one who must correct it.
Fear can remain when the self who must overcome it no longer forms.
The fear still occurs through a particular body, history, and situation.
Maya experiences the assignment through what school and achievement have come to mean in her life.
Another student may experience the same assignment differently.
I use standpoint for the experience as it occurs through these particular relations.
Standpoint is the experience itself, not a separate observer receiving it.
Fear can have this felt perspective without forming a separate self who owns it and must bring it under control.
Noncompletion occurs when claiming becomes recognizable without forming a separate owner.
In the case of fear, what seemed to be a self controlling the feeling becomes recognizable as the effort to escape it.
The division between fear and the self who must overcome it is not renewed.
No separate observer decides to end it.
Fear can remain, and memory and knowledge can still guide practical action.
In DI, the apparent owner of experience is a social construction.
Through relationships, children learn to treat feelings as things a separate self has and must manage.
This claiming forms the claimer.

Caregivers address the child as someone who feels and wants, respond to distress, and reflect feelings through voice and expression. Reddy (2008) describes infants' awareness of others' attention in such exchanges. Gergely and Watson (1996) propose that caregivers' mirroring helps infants recognize their emotional states.
text.formatted: Caregivers address the child as someone who feels and wants, respond to distress, and reflect feelings through voice and expression. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Reddy (2008)</ref> describes infants' awareness of others' attention in such exchanges. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Gergely and Watson (1996)</ref> propose that caregivers' mirroring helps infants recognize their emotional states.

text.text: DI suggests that these exchanges can also make it familiar to experience a feeling as belonging to a self who stands apart from it.
Language can reinforce this separation.
A child hears "You are frightened" and learns to say "I am frightened," acquiring grammatical patterns through everyday exchanges (Tomasello, 2003).
text.formatted: A child hears "You are frightened" and learns to say "I am frightened," acquiring grammatical patterns through everyday exchanges <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Tomasello, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Parents and children also build accounts of past experiences together, and the child learns to speak of past events as things that happened to "me" (Nelson & Fivush, 2004).
text.formatted: Parents and children also build accounts of past experiences together, and the child learns to speak of past events as things that happened to "me" <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Nelson & Fivush, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Such language can simply describe what happened or how someone feels, but it can also present a separate self who has that experience and must manage it.
DI proposes that children can learn to address and judge themselves as others have addressed and judged them.
A child repeatedly told to stop being afraid may later think, "I should not feel this way.
I must get rid of this fear."
The demand now seems to come from a self who stands apart from the feeling.
Yet that self is the learned activity of judging fear and demanding its end.
What began as a demand between people continues as an apparent struggle between a self and its experience.
Writing an assignment or learning a skill takes clock time.

I use psychological time for the division thought makes between "what I am" and "what I must become, recover, or preserve." Krishnamurti (1969) argued that the effort to overcome this conflict only sustains it.
text.formatted: I use psychological time for the division thought makes between "what I am" and "what I must become, recover, or preserve." <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Krishnamurti (1969)</ref> argued that the effort to overcome this conflict only sustains it.

text.text: If I must become fearless, the future I want is defined by the fear I want to escape now.
For Maya, "I should already be further along" made her life seem late.
The comparison formed the self who was behind and had to catch up.
The change she wanted lay in the future, but trying to reach it kept that self and its problem active now.
A person who believes they must recover their old happiness compares life now with what they remember.
The past supplies the image of a future they feel they must reach.
Present pleasure can also become something that must continue.
Thought imagines its loss, and the effort to preserve it brings fear into what is pleasurable.
In both cases, the demand forms the self who must recover happiness or prevent its loss.
The past can also seem to rule out change: "I have always been this way, and I always will be."
The person treats their past as proof that they cannot change.
This judgment defines the self as someone whose future is already settled.
In each of these examples, the past and future enter only as images that thought forms now, and the judgment that defines the self is made in the present.
Psychological time is therefore not a stretch of time the self must cross but the conflict itself, and the self forms each time thought measures the actual against an image.

This is why Krishnamurti (1969) held that this conflict cannot end through a gradual effort to become free of it: working toward freedom over time is one more movement from "what is" toward "what should be," and it keeps that self in place.
text.formatted: This is why <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Krishnamurti (1969)</ref> held that this conflict cannot end through a gradual effort to become free of it: working toward freedom over time is one more movement from "what is" toward "what should be," and it keeps that self in place.

text.text: Clock time remains necessary: Maya's assignment still takes hours to write, and she can plan her work and continue while afraid.
What need not continue is the demand that the outcome establish who she is or decide when her life can begin.
Efforts to end a self-problem can keep it going.
A setback seems to confirm "I need fixing," while improvement becomes proof that "I am finally putting myself right."
Either way, the outcome remains a judgment about the self.
For Maya, each unfinished assignment became further evidence that something was wrong with her.
I could also use her progress to judge my competence.
Completing the work and helping her complete it could then become ways of proving ourselves.
Wanting shows this clearly.
A therapist asks, "What do you want?"
and the client says, "I want to be free of fear."
In centering, the wish for a future without fear forms a self who is still trapped in fear and must escape it.
Fear itself becomes the threat to escape.
The anxious effort to escape is experienced as a separate self responsible for ending the fear.
Yet this effort is fear continuing as the attempt to become free of itself.
At the centering grain, the relation can be stated directly: To want to be free of fear is the fear.
Understanding can also become part of the struggle.
Maya understood why she procrastinated and believed she should therefore be able to stop.
Her understanding became another reason to judge herself.
A client may learn why they feel anxious and how to reduce it, and that knowledge may be accurate and useful.
If staying in control is necessary to remain the person they want to be, each return of fear threatens that identity.
They may feel less anxious while continuing to experience a separate self who has fear and must manage it.
What they have learned can still help when this self no longer forms.
U. G. Krishnamurti (1982 Krishnamurti ( , 1988) ) argues that efforts to free oneself from the self can continue the activity they reject.
text.formatted: U. G. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Krishnamurti (1982</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Krishnamurti ( , 1988) )</ref> argues that efforts to free oneself from the self can continue the activity they reject.

text.text: DI is not exempt.
When "I must become permanently uncentered" becomes the goal, inquiry turns into a demand to reach an ideal state and stay there.
The self forms again as the one who must achieve that state and prevent its loss.
Practical help remains important.
Skills or medication may let someone face a difficulty that would otherwise overwhelm them.
DI asks whether using this help also forms a self who appears to stand apart from the feeling and must control it.
The same study plan can help someone finish a paper while also becoming a way to prove they are not a failure.
The paper can still receive full attention when completing it no longer has to establish who the person is or become a condition they must meet before they can finally be happy.
The encounter with Maya shows how this possibility can arise during the work itself.
I return to a session with Maya in which an unfinished paper had become evidence that she was the problem.
She described losing most of her morning worrying about it.
She had opened the document, imagined her work would be inadequate, looked at social media, and gone back to bed.
"I should be further along by now," she said.
"I keep doing this to myself.
I'm the reason my life isn't moving."
Maya's struggle was organized in psychological time.
She measured her life against the life she believed she should already have.
The comparison made her present life unacceptable, while catching up promised a future in which she could finally be at ease.
I asked, "What do you mean by further along?"
"I should be finished with school.
I should have a career.
Everyone else seems to be getting somewhere."
"And what would be different for you if you were there?"
"I could relax.
I could feel good about my life instead of always trying to get it together."
Maya began explaining these expectations through her father and what achievement had meant in their family.
I asked, "When you remember what he expected, what do you expect of yourself now?"
"That I should be doing more.
That I am wasting what I could have been."
As she pictured her classmates completing their work, she described tightness under her ribs and heat in her face.
What she had learned about achievement was already at work as the meaning of the unfinished paper and the fear.
Her remembered expectations, imagined future, and sense of being behind belonged to this same experience.
I asked, "What happens to the life you have while you try to reach that life?"
"It feels like it is on hold.
I have to sort all this out before I can enjoy anything."
"What do you have to sort out?"
"Me.
I have to stop being like this."
She began listing the paper, her degree, her relationship, and her age.
I drew attention to how each difficulty had become another reason she needed fixing.
"One unfinished paper has become your whole life," I said.
"And now you're the person who must fix it.
What do you do when you try to make yourself right?"
"I look at what I should be doing.
I tell myself to stop wasting time.
I try to push myself."
"And what happens as you do that?"
"I become more frightened.
There is so much I have to change."
"You push yourself to change because you are afraid of staying as you are," I said.
"Then you tell yourself that your whole life needs fixing, and you become more frightened.
You're trying to get away from fear, but maybe trying to escape is what keeps you stuck."
We examined the effort she experienced as the self trying to bring everything under control.
She compared her life with the life she should have, judged herself for falling short, and tried to escape that condition.
Ownership can also form without a judgment of personal failure.
"My anxiety is ruining my life" may describe serious limitations that need treatment.
However, complete freedom from anxiety may also have become a condition for beginning the life the client wants.
They may postpone choices they could make while anxious because they believe they must first become someone without fear.
The self who cannot yet live takes shape through this demand.
DI examines this requirement alongside the anxiety's actual limitations.
Inquiry concerns both the help the person needs and what they expect relief to make possible.
Maya's report raises a question about the seeing itself.
If she recognized how hurt was becoming a problem about who she was, had another self stepped back to observe it?
Giving the task to a better observer would leave the same difficulty in place.
Maya would need to observe herself correctly, and failing could become another reason to judge herself.
DI therefore needs to explain how this pattern can be recognized without a separate self taking charge of ending it.
Maya may be thinking about how to answer her partner while still hearing what is said and feeling hurt.
In DI, all of this is consciousness occurring.
She does not also have to think, "I am hearing this," for the words to be heard and understood. Dretske (1993) and Tye (1999) likewise argue that experience can occur without awareness of having it.
text.formatted: She does not also have to think, "I am hearing this," for the words to be heard and understood. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Dretske (1993)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Tye (1999)</ref> likewise argue that experience can occur without awareness of having it.

text.text: DI explains this through recognition: knowledge is operating as the experience, whether or not a further thought about experiencing it occurs.
If Maya then notices her effort to put herself right, that effort has itself become something recognized.
Recognizing the effort does not require a separate observer standing outside it.
Nor does it necessarily form a self responsible for ending it.
The hurt had seemed to reveal a fact about someone already there: Maya ruined relationships and therefore had a life to repair.
What became recognizable was that the demand for repair was also defining her as that person.
The self who needed repair was this pattern of treating hurt as a verdict about her and demanding that she change.
Recognition could include this pattern just as it included the hurt and the conflict with her partner.
Maya could also respond, DI uses visibility for an event in which claiming becomes recognizable without completing into ownership.
Maya could recognize how hurt was becoming a verdict about her without renewing the demand to repair her entire life.
The owner had seemed to exist before this demand, but it was being formed through it.
When the demand was no longer renewed, neither was that owner.
Visibility and noncompletion describe the same event: the claiming becomes recognizable and does not form an owner-owned division.
No separate observer first sees the division and then acts to remove it.
Put sharply: noncompletion is not something that happens to someone.
It is the nothappening of the someone.
The someone in this statement is the particular owner formed within the encounter.
Maya remained present and responsive, able to remember the conflict and discuss her relationship.
The demand to repair her entire life was no longer defining who she was.
The person continued, along with the capacities and relationships through which she could act.
Her hurt also remained situated within her life.
It still concerned her partner, and her history still informed what the conflict meant.
Knowledge continued as this recognizable experience, including its felt perspective.
She could feel hurt and consider the conflict without renewing the claim that the hurt made her someone who ruined relationships.
Using I to describe this event does not establish that an owner had taken charge of the seeing.
"I saw what was happening" ordinarily identifies the person telling us about it.
We need to understand what they noticed and what they felt responsible for doing.
The retelling is also a present encounter.
A client may worry, "I need to know that I really understood," making the recollection another test they must pass.
That demand is occurring now; it need not describe the earlier experience.
Their report allows therapist and client to examine the difference.
I propose that insight into this claiming changes the knowledge through which a self and its problem form.
Maya may again feel afraid about unfinished work, and the demand to change herself may begin again.
However, that demand now occurs through knowledge altered by the earlier insight.
The demand may no longer form that owner as readily.
It may arise without forming an owner at all.
This change does not depend on remembering the earlier encounter or trying to reproduce it.
A lasting change in this struggle does not mean that centering has ended throughout Maya's life.
Other difficulties may still involve a self who must change or preserve an experience.
The earlier insight may make these demands easier to recognize as they arise.
Therapist and client can examine whether she can address unfinished work without first having to correct who she is.
If the same struggle continues unchanged, remembering or explaining the insight would not establish a lasting change.
Maya's encounter can be understood through more than one therapeutic account.
Several of the approaches considered here already treat the self as formed rather than given.
I ask one question of each: when it works as intended, what happens to the self who appears to stand apart from experience as the one who has it and must manage it?
A person's relationship to a thought or feeling can change while this apparent owner continues to form.
DI examines how the observer forms within the activity it seems to observe (J. Krishnamurti, 1969).
text.formatted: DI examines how the observer forms within the activity it seems to observe (J. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Krishnamurti, 1969)</ref>.

text.text: In noncompletion, that formation becomes recognizable without completing into an owner and what it owns.
Rogers described a relationship in which the therapist is genuine and responds with unconditional positive regard and empathic understanding (Rogers, 1957 (Rogers, , 1961)).
text.formatted: Rogers described a relationship in which the therapist is genuine and responds with unconditional positive regard and empathic understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Rogers, 1957</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Rogers, , 1961))</ref>.

text.text: In this relationship, conditions of worth can loosen.
The client can acknowledge feelings that once threatened their self-concept, and how they see themselves can come to agree more closely with what they feel.
A client may admit feeling afraid without having to earn the therapist's acceptance by becoming fearless.
Person-centered therapy already addresses the conditions through which clients judge their worth, including those the therapist's expectations introduce.
Contemporary person-centered writing also challenges the view that the approach treats people as isolated from social relations (Cornelius-White, 2025).
The change concerns how the client understands themselves in relation to what they feel.
They may now see themselves as someone who is allowed to feel afraid, rather than someone who must be fearless to be acceptable.
Fear can be acknowledged within this changed selfconcept.
DI asks how the image of oneself is being formed.
The thought "I am someone who accepts fear" can give the apparent self a position to maintain.
In noncompletion, Maya can feel afraid without having to become either the one who overcomes fear or the one who accepts it.
A person-centered relationship can provide conditions in which this event becomes possible.
Gestalt therapy understands self as the process of contact between organism and environment (Perls et al., 1951).
text.formatted: Gestalt therapy understands self as the process of contact between organism and environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Perls et al., 1951)</ref>.

text.text: Field-oriented work explains how self takes shape within the situation, including the relations through which therapist and client participate (Robine, 2011; Cavaleri & Iacono Isidoro, 2026).
text.formatted: Field-oriented work explains how self takes shape within the situation, including the relations through which therapist and client participate <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Robine, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Cavaleri & Iacono Isidoro, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A Gestalt account would understand Maya's fear within these relations, including my part in them.
Self is already being explained as activity within a field, rather than as someone who exists before contact begins.
Perls et al. (1951) describe identification and alienation as functions of contact: what is accepted as one's own and what is set aside.
Gestalt treats this identification as part of how self functions.
DI asks whether the activity forms a self who appears separate from the feeling and responsible for changing it.
This division cannot be inferred from the term identification alone.
If fear becomes the condition of someone who must eliminate it before life can continue, the demand forms that apparent owner.
When claiming does not complete, Maya can still feel fear, remain involved, and act.
Noncompletion concerns this owner-owned division; it does not mean an unfinished gestalt or withdrawal from contact.

Decentering concerns changes in how people relate to thoughts and feelings. Bernstein et al. (2015) identify three processes: meta-awareness, or noticing experience as it occurs; disidentification, or experiencing a thought or feeling without equating it with oneself; and reduced reactivity to thought content.
text.formatted: Decentering concerns changes in how people relate to thoughts and feelings. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bernstein et al. (2015)</ref> identify three processes: meta-awareness, or noticing experience as it occurs; disidentification, or experiencing a thought or feeling without equating it with oneself; and reduced reactivity to thought content.

text.text: A thought can be noticed as a mental event without being taken as a fact or a definition of who one is.
Maya's thought that she was failing could still arise while having less influence on how she approached the assignment.
Decentering is also studied as a momentary state in daily life (Naragon-Gainey et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Decentering is also studied as a momentary state in daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Naragon-Gainey et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Suddenness does not distinguish DI.
The question is whether the observing position continues.
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) addresses related concerns through defusion and self-as-context (Hayes et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) addresses related concerns through defusion and self-as-context <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hayes et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Defusion lets a thought remain present without dictating what the person does.
Self-as-context is the perspective from which thoughts and feelings are noticed, explained through learned relations such as the distinctions between I and you or here and there.
When ACT works, the person acts on their values with difficult thoughts and feelings present, observed from a context that remains stable while its contents change.
ACT does not treat this context as an inner entity, and neither ACT nor DI treats the center as a substance.
Even so, self-as-context is a sense of self distinct from and larger than its contents; in ACT's chessboard metaphor, the board holds the pieces and is not any of them (Hayes et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Even so, self-as-context is a sense of self distinct from and larger than its contents; in ACT's chessboard metaphor, the board holds the pieces and is not any of them <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hayes et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In Bernstein et al.'s (2015) model, likewise, the one who disidentifies from a thought remains as the one who notices it.
DI asks how this observing self forms.
ACT's self-as-content means the descriptions and evaluations a person holds about themselves.
DI uses experienced content more broadly.
It includes the felt sense of being the one who observes, as well as the thought or feeling observed.
A quiet or accepting witness is therefore part of what requires explanation.
When Maya recognized hurt becoming a verdict about her, no observer first stepped back and then withheld the verdict.
The claiming became recognizable and did not complete.
DI does not retain a witness as the self to which the rest of experience appears.
Cognitive therapy examines how interpretations and beliefs shape feelings and behavior.
Clients evaluate thoughts about particular situations and broader beliefs about themselves, called
Constructivist psychotherapy treats the self as formed rather than given. Kelly (1955) described how people use personal constructs, or ways of interpreting events, to make sense of their lives.
text.formatted: Constructivist psychotherapy treats the self as formed rather than given. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Kelly (1955)</ref> described how people use personal constructs, or ways of interpreting events, to make sense of their lives.

text.text: The self is one such construct. Mahoney (2003) describes the self as an ongoing organizing process. Neimeyer (2009) explains how therapy reconstructs meaning when a person's way of making sense of life has broken down. Gergen (2009) locates the self within relationship: it is formed through what people do together.
text.formatted: The self is one such construct. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Mahoney (2003)</ref> describes the self as an ongoing organizing process. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Neimeyer (2009)</ref> explains how therapy reconstructs meaning when a person's way of making sense of life has broken down. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Gergen (2009)</ref> locates the self within relationship: it is formed through what people do together.

text.text: On this view, the bounded individual is a cultural tradition rather than a fact.
Narrative therapy helps people distinguish themselves from their problems and develop a preferred account of their lives (White & Epston, 1990).
text.formatted: Narrative therapy helps people distinguish themselves from their problems and develop a preferred account of their lives <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(White & Epston, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Anxiety can affect someone's life without defining who they are.
Recent humanistic counseling scholarship also questions the assumption of a stable, authentic self (Lemberger-Truelove et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recent humanistic counseling scholarship also questions the assumption of a stable, authentic self <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lemberger-Truelove et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: DI shares the view that the self is formed in relation.
DI's account extends to inherited and bodily ways of recognizing, including experience before language.
A child can see colors before learning to name them, and a gazelle may experience danger through inherited capacities.
Neither experience requires a story about it.
Centering can occur without someone telling or revising a story.
Externalization also distinguishes the person from the problem, allowing the person to oppose its influence.
DI asks how telling the story or opposing the problem can form an apparent self who stands apart from the activity as the one directing it.
When claiming does not complete, the person can remember what happened and describe their life without forming a self whose position the account must secure.
The ability to tell a story continues.
The owner whose position must be protected does not form.

The Formation of the Sufferer 29 Therapy within any of these approaches may provide conditions in which claiming becomes recognizable, but noncompletion cannot be secured as an achievement of the self.
U. G. Krishnamurti's (1982 Krishnamurti's ( , 1988) ) criticism of efforts to become free of the self therefore applies to DI as well.
text.formatted: U. G. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Krishnamurti's (1982</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Krishnamurti's ( , 1988) )</ref> criticism of efforts to become free of the self therefore applies to DI as well.

text.text: DI explains how the apparent owner takes shape through claiming and how this claiming can become recognizable without forming that owner.
The therapist's participation in Maya's impasse has implications for supervision.
A trainee may describe a client who has not followed through on agreed changes: "I've reflected the pattern, made plans with her, and challenged the avoidance.
She still won't move.
I think I'm failing her."
This composite draws on situations that recur in my supervision.
In the trainee's account, the client becomes the resistant one who must change, while the trainee's competence depends on making that change happen.
My wish to provide an answer can also become a need to prove that I am the expert.
The client's progress is being asked to establish who each of us is.
Direct instruction or corrective feedback may still be needed.
The supervisor remains responsible for assessing risk, evaluating competence, and protecting client welfare.
Inquiry asks whether the need to prove ourselves is limiting our understanding of the client's goals, cultural context, or relationship with the therapist.
Culture helps shape what becomes recognizable and what a person feels required to do.
Family expectations may make disagreement feel like disloyalty, while expectations about age and achievement may make unfinished work feel like falling behind.
These meanings belong to how the situation is experienced.

Accounts in psychological anthropology and cultural psychology describe how self-understanding varies with social relationships and cultural meanings (Geertz, 1973; Markus & Kitayama, 1991; Rosaldo, 1984).
text.formatted: Accounts in psychological anthropology and cultural psychology describe how self-understanding varies with social relationships and cultural meanings <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Geertz, 1973;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Markus & Kitayama, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Rosaldo, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Within DI, these expectations can also define the one who must meet them.
The demand to be a loyal family member, for example, may make disagreement a defect to correct and the person someone who must suppress it to remain acceptable.
Power also shapes the positions people are made to occupy.
A person may face discrimination or danger, and vigilance may accurately reflect those conditions.
Institutions can keep imposing a position even when the person questions it.
DI therefore examines both how a position becomes something the person must defend or escape and how others continue to impose it.
Changing the client's interpretation cannot by itself remove these conditions.
Protection or collective action may be needed.
Cultural affiliations and shared histories can support such action.
Inquiry gives the therapist no basis for deciding that a client should relinquish a valued identity or justified anger.
The client's account of harm deserves attention whether or not the demand to defend who they are is renewed.
Deconstructive Inquiry examines how a difficulty and the self who must resolve it take shape together.
For Maya, unfinished work became evidence that she needed fixing.
She judged her present life against the life she believed she should already be living.
This comparison The Formation of the Sufferer 31 organized psychological time and defined her as the one who was behind.
The therapist's effort to help could reinforce that demand.
DI proposes that this pattern can become recognizable without renewing the ownerowned division.
Recognition continues: Maya can still feel afraid and understand what needs attention.
What is no longer renewed is the demand that her work must repair who she is.
I propose that insight also changes how a similar difficulty is recognized later, without requiring Maya to remember or recreate the earlier encounter.
When this division ends, the person continues, with their body, memory, relationships, and capacity to act.
The sufferer, the one whose life depends on solving the problem, does not form.
The freedom is not for someone.
It is the absence of the one who needed freedom.
core beliefs, through evidence and practical experience (Beck, 1976) The word belief can refer to a practical expectation, such as expecting a chair to support us.
text.formatted: core beliefs, through evidence and practical experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Beck, 1976)</ref> The word belief can refer to a practical expectation, such as expecting a chair to support us.

text.text: That expectation draws on knowledge and can be mistaken.
Psychological belief gives a conclusion another role: it becomes a position to maintain or defend.
Maya can know that she completed an assignment without taking it as proof that she is a competent person.
If the accomplishment establishes "I am competent," the record is now defining the person she takes herself to be.
Holding that conclusion forms the believer whose position it is.
This can concern more than personal worth.
A belief may promise certainty or establish what must happen before life can begin.
J. Krishnamurti (1954) examines how identification with belief offers psychological security.
text.formatted: J. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Krishnamurti (1954)</ref> examines how identification with belief offers psychological security.

text.text: DI explains this identification as centering: the believing forms the believer.
Thought divides into the belief and an apparent self who holds it.
This self seems to have existed before the belief, but it takes shape through the believing.
Cognitive restructuring asks whether a belief is accurate and useful.
DI asks how believing forms its apparent holder.
Replacing "I am a failure" with "I am competent" can be an accurate and helpful change in a core belief while the self continues as its holder.
When the claiming does not complete, Maya can recognize the thought without holding it as a belief about herself.
She can remember what she has accomplished and use that knowledge to prepare.
The work she has completed no longer has to prove who she is.

One description concerns what the body detects and how it responds.
I use registration to mean that the body detects something happening within it or around it.
When a person is afraid, their heart may beat faster and their chest may tighten as the body prepares to respond.
The bodily-registration grain describes this detection and response.
These responses draw on inherited capacities and can be shaped by previous experience.
Some bodily changes occur without the person feeling them.
A racing heart can also occur during excitement.
To understand the encounter as fear, we also need to consider what the situation means to the person and how it feels.
Consider an employee whose heart races when a supervisor asks about their work.
They understand the words through their knowledge of language.
If the supervisor has often criticized them, they may hear the question as another criticism and feel afraid.
Their knowledge is already operating as both what the question means and how it feels.
I call this recognition: knowledge operating as experience.
another.
Distinguishing them helps us examine what changes when the struggle ends.
The body can still respond and the person can still feel afraid.
What no longer forms is the self whose life depends on controlling that fear.
The person is also an organized pattern of relations.
Their bodily life and history with others shape what they can recognize and do.
Memory and responsibility belong to this organization and are shaped by knowledge and culture.
These relations can continue when the division between an experience and its apparent owner no longer forms.
The person who continues is this bodily and social organization, not an underlying self revealed when conflict disappears.
For example, Maya can remember an agreement and recognize that her partner relied on it.
If she breaks it, the consequences still matter, and she can acknowledge what she did and make amends.
Her responsibility concerns what she agreed to and how breaking it affects her partner.
Responding to that harm need not become a demand to repair a defective self.
The ending of that self-problem does not erase what happened or remove the need to respond.
asked, "Who is trying to end the fear?"
"It feels like I am trying to make myself do something."
"What is that 'I' doing right now?"
"Comparing.
Telling myself I should be different.
Trying to get away from how I feel."
"The comparison makes you the one who is behind," I said.
"The effort to catch up feels like a separate self directing it.
But that self is the effort itself."
"But the paper still is not written."
"Yes.
Writing it takes time.
Why do you have to become someone different before you can write it?"
"Because I keep thinking that once I'm different, I can finally get on with it."
"And that day keeps moving ahead of you, like chasing the horizon."
Maya was quiet for a moment.
"I keep pursuing a life I'm supposed to have, and then I'm the person who's failing to get there.
Even when I try to fix it, I'm doing the same thing."
"What's happening as you see that now?"
"I'm still nervous about the paper," she said.
"But the panic is gone.
I don't have a whole life to fix first."
I understand this change through DI's account of noncompletion.
Maya recognized how the demand to reach a different life formed the self whose present life was unacceptable.
That demand no longer formed an owner responsible for escaping the present condition.
She had not given herself an instruction to stop comparing.
The comparison and the apparent controller were recognizable as the same activity.
The inquiry continued with the paper.
I asked what she wanted to explain and where she was having difficulty.
She identified a paragraph on the second article, and we worked on what it needed to say.
Her knowledge and abilities remained available.
Writing still took time, but it no longer had to make her into the person she believed she should become.
The paper needed a paragraph, not a different person.
The following week, describing a conflict with her partner, Maya said, "This proves I ruin every relationship."
Then she recognized what that conclusion was doing.
"There is the The Formation of the Sufferer 20 whole life to repair again.
I am hurt, and suddenly it means I have always ruined things and always will."
A remembered past was becoming a settled future.
Maya could recognize this demand without trying to recreate the earlier insight.
I asked what the hurt was like now.
"It's still here," she said, "but it isn't telling me who I am."
She still felt hurt and needed to consider what had happened with her partner, but the hurt no longer required repairing the person she believed it proved her to be.
The conflict needed a conversation, not a repaired life.
Structural Attention Structural attention means following how a difficulty comes to define the self who must resolve it.
This includes the standard against which the difficulty is judged and what the person feels must happen before life can be acceptable.
In Maya's case, fear became evidence that she was failing, leaving her responsible for repairing herself.
My response could add to that demand if I needed her improvement to prove my competence.
Attending to this relation includes how we are defining each other through the work.
The client's speech gives us a way to explore what the difficulty has come to require.
Consider "I should be over this by now."
The person may be comparing how they feel with how they believe they ought to feel after this much time.
Their present life may then feel held up until they meet that expectation.
If continued distress means personal failure, the feeling has become another reason to judge and correct themselves.
Words such as should and must can draw attention to a standard the person feels responsible for meeting.
To understand that standard, the clinician needs to know what the client means in the particular encounter.
"I failed this examination and need a plan" can describe a task that deserves attention.
"This failure proves that I am a failure, and I must repair my life" asks more of the plan.
It must change who the person is as well as improve their preparation.
The examination result is the same, but its consequences for the person's sense of self differ.
Now I have to stop doing this."
Understanding what happens can become another demand to change oneself.
might ask, "Could we look at what the client's lack of progress has come to mean about you?
I'm also noticing how quickly I feel I have to be the one with the answer."
We can examine this demand while reviewing the recording and deciding what help the client needs.
A formulation can guide treatment without its success having to prove the trainee's competence.

She can then consider what this assignment requires and decide how to begin.

The comparison with DI depends on what is meant by belief.

table.html: Term Definition Self-problem relation The organization of experience in which a difficulty becomes the problem of a self who must resolve it, and that self takes shape through the demand to resolve it. Centering The claiming of experience as the condition of a self who must change or protect it. The claiming forms the claimer. Psychological belief A conclusion held as a position the self must maintain or defend, as distinct from a practical expectation. The believing forms the believer. Ownership (owner- The apparent separation, produced when claiming completes, owned division) between a self and the experience it has and must manage. Noncompletion The claiming becomes recognizable without completing into ownership. Feeling and practical understanding can continue while the owner does not form. Visibility The same event named from the side of recognition: the claiming is seen as it occurs, without a separate observer taking charge of ending it. Psychological time The division thought makes between what I am and what I must become, recover, or preserve.
